cves.summary: rustls 0.23.44 and 0.23.45 contain an information disclosure vulnerability that sends application data buffered before the handshake completes to the client-facing server when Encrypted Client Hello is rejected. Because start_traffic() queues plaintext from ClientConnection::writer() before sending the ech_required alert, the authenticated public_name server receives data intended for the inner server.

rustls before 0.23.46 contains a key exchange downgrade vulnerability that allows network attackers to poison the per-server-name key-exchange group record via an unauthenticated ServerHello. Attackers can answer one connection with a ServerHello selecting X25519, causing later ClientHellos to send only classical shares and lose post-quantum confidentiality.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto from 0.3.1 before 0.26.1 contains a denial of service vulnerability in BinEncoder that allows remote attackers to exhaust CPU through quadratic-time name compression. Attackers can send malicious DNS messages with many records that add many candidate labels and trigger repeated linear scans during encoding, amplifying CPU exhaustion.

Hickory DNS hickory-proto 0.1 through 0.25.0-alpha.3 and hickory-net before 0.26.2 contain a DNSSEC validation bypass because the validator verifies an RRSIG against the DNSKEY of whatever name appears in its Signer's Name field without checking that this name is the zone containing the RRset. Attackers controlling any secure zone can produce valid signatures over arbitrary records in unrelated zones, which resolvers, recursors, and clients using DnssecDnsHandle accept as authenticated.

rustls before 0.23.46 contains an uncontrolled memory allocation flaw in its optional Brotli certificate decompression, which limits decompressed output size but accepts an input-selected large history window. Malicious peers can send a certificate with a five-byte Brotli header requesting up to 1 GiB before authentication, aborting Brotli-enabled clients or client-authenticating servers whose allocator cannot satisfy the request.

hickory-proto and hickory-resolver 0.26.0 before 0.26.2, hickory-server 0.25.0-alpha.1 before 0.26.2, and hickory-recursor 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.26.0-alpha.1 fail to canonicalize IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses when checking deny_answers, deny_server, or AccessControlSet rules. Attackers can use IPv4-mapped addresses to evade answer filtering, trigger queries to denied nameservers, or reach hickory-server library deployments on dual-stack IPv6 sockets from denied clients.

imgproxy 3.3.0 before 4.0.17 contains an out-of-bounds heap read and write in the ICO loader's BMP header reconstruction (vips_foreign_load_ico_header in vips/icoload.c) when an ICO entry declares a tiny data size, causing unvalidated header fields to be read and written past the allocated buffer. Unauthenticated remote attackers can supply a crafted ICO image to corrupt adjacent heap chunk metadata, triggering a glibc abort that crashes the worker.

Hickory DNS hickory-resolver 0.26.0-beta.1 before 0.26.2 contains an unbounded retry loop in NameServerPool::try_send, which re-queues truncated (TC) responses without checking the answering transport or counting iterations. A malicious authoritative server returning TC=1 on every transport keeps the resolver spinning on a persistent TCP connection until the 5-second request deadline expires, causing resource exhaustion.

Rustls before 0.23.46 and 0.24.0-dev.1 before 0.24.0-dev.2 contains an information disclosure vulnerability where derived Debug formatting of client session values exposes secret key material. Custom ClientSessionStore implementations that log Tls12ClientSessionValue or Tls13ClientSessionValue can leak TLS 1.2 master secrets or TLS 1.3 resumption PSKs to log readers.

The hickory-dns recursor in hickory-recursor 0.25.0-alpha.3 through 0.25.2 and hickory-resolver 0.26.0-alpha.1 before 0.26.2 iterates every out-of-bailiwick NS target lacking glue in a referral without any per-query work budget. Remote attackers can serve such referrals to force A and AAAA lookups per target, amplifying traffic against remote servers or exhausting recursor resources.
Buffer overflow in Norton Antivirus for Exchange (NavExchange) allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a .zip file that contains long file names.

bb_smilies.php and bbcode_ref.php in PHP-Nuke 4.4 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files and gain PHP administrator privileges by inserting a null character and .. (dot dot) sequences into a malformed username argument.
opendir.php script in PHP-Nuke allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files by specifying the filename as an argument to the requesturl parameter.

Windows 98 and Windows 2000 Java clients allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a Java applet that opens a large number of UDP sockets, which prevents the host from establishing any additional UDP connections, and possibly causes a crash.
Buffer overflow in QNX RTP 5.60 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service and possibly execute arbitrary commands via a large number of arguments to the stat command.

Oracle Java Virtual Machine (JVM ) for Oracle 8.1.7 and Oracle Application Server 9iAS Release 1.0.2.0.1 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via the .jsp and .sqljsp file extensions when the server is configured to use the <<ALL FILES>> FilePermission.
mandb in the man-db package before 2.3.16-3 allows local users to overwrite arbitrary files via the command line options (1) -u or (2) -c, which do not drop privileges and follow symlinks.
Buffer overflows in Linux CUPS before 1.1.6 may allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

Apache on Red Hat Linux with with the UserDir directive enabled generates different error codes when a username exists and there is no public_html directory and when the username does not exist, which could allow remote attackers to determine valid usernames on the server.
Buffer overflow in xlib in XFree 3.3.x possibly allows local users to execute arbitrary commands via a long DISPLAY environment variable or a -display command line parameter.

mailfile.cgi CGI program in MailFile 1.10 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files by specifying the target file name in the "filename" parameter in a POST request, which is then sent by email to the address specified in the "email" parameter.
bbd server in Big Brother System and Network Monitor before 1.5c2 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via the "&" shell metacharacter.

Directory traversal vulnerability in Drummond Miles A1Stats prior to 1.6 allows a remote attacker to read arbitrary files via a '..' (dot dot) attack in (1) a1disp2.cgi, (2) a1disp3.cgi, or (3) a1disp4.cgi.
a1disp.cgi program in Drummond Miles A1Stats prior to 1.6 allows a remote attacker to execute commands via a specially crafted URL which includes shell metacharacters.
ElectroSystems Engineering Inc. ElectroComm 2.0 and earlier allows a remote attacker to create a denial of service via large (> 160000 character) strings sent to port 23.
Vulnerability in Interchange 4.8.6, 4.8.3, and other versions, when running in INET mode, allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files.
ICMP information such as (1) netmask and (2) timestamp is allowed from arbitrary hosts.
SQL injection vulnerability in category.asp in A-CART Pro and A-CART 2.0 allows remote attackers to gain privileges via the catcode parameter.

### Impact
An application that passes attacker-controlled data into joi's custom message configuration (`messages()`, `message()`, `prefs({ messages })`, `Joi.extend({ messages })` or `rule({ message })`) lets the attacker write properties onto `Object.prototype`, where every object in the process then inherits them. A key named `__proto__` was treated as a language name, and the code reused the object it found at that key, which resolves to the prototype rather than to a new own property; a key named `constructor` did the same to the `Object` function's statics. A consuming application that gates on the mere presence of a property (`if (user.isAdmin)`) can be made to take the wrong branch for every object it inspects.

This is not reachable from data that joi validates. Custom messages are schema-construction configuration, normally written by the application developer. Exploitation therefore requires an application that feeds untrusted input straight into schema construction.

### Patches
Upgrade to version 18.2.5 or 17.13.6.

### Workarounds
Do not pass untrusted input into `messages()`, `message()`, `prefs({ messages })`, `Joi.extend({ messages })` or `rule({ message })`. Or validate that they don't contain any `__proto__` or `constructor` property.

cwe.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution')

cves.summary:
### Impact

Applications are affected only if a schema renames keys with a regular-expression source and a `Joi.expression()` / `Joi.x()` target that interpolates the pattern's own match data, combined with `{ multiple: true }`, for example `.rename(/^x-(.+)$/, Joi.x('{#1}'), { multiple: true })`. Because the target is rendered from the matched input key, an attacker who controls input keys can send `x-__proto__` with an object value and make the rename target render as `__proto__`, which sets the prototype of the object joi returns instead of creating a key on it. The global `Object.prototype` is not modified, so the effect is confined to the object returned by that one `validate()` call.

Schemas using a static string rename target are not affected, and neither are schemas left on the default `{ multiple: false }`.

### Patches

Versions 17.13.5 and 18.2.4 have been released to address the issue.

### Workarounds

1. Replace the template rename target with a static string target.
2. Keep the template but make the capture unable to produce `__proto__`, using a negative lookahead: `.rename(/^x-(?!__proto__$)(.+)$/, Joi.x('{#1}'), { multiple: true })`
3. Drop { multiple: true } from the rename, which stops the rename before the assignment.

### Summary
A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.

### Details

[Section 3.4 of the RFC 8628 spec](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628#section-3.4) says that the token endpoint should take in `device_code` as a required parameter.`DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does not perform any validation of `device_code`. `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` should be validating that `device_code` was passed in as a parameter and that it is valid, similar to how `AuthorizationCodeGrant.validate_token_request` does the checks [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L446) and [here](https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/blob/a015b446622f2b925517501fe484c10eff7a83c0/oauthlib/oauth2/rfc6749/grant_types/authorization_code.py#L483).

I would like to propose a new method be added to `RequestValidator` called `validate_device_code` that is similar to the `validate_code` method and is called inside of `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request`.

### PoC
Create an implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` that returns `True` if the client's `client_type` is `"public"`. You would find yourself in this scenario because there's another issue with `DeviceCodeGrant.validate_token_request` where it doesn't properly handle public clients (see https://github.com/oauthlib/oauthlib/issues/919).

Create a client that has a `client_type` of `"public"` and set it's `grant_type` to `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"`.

With this implementation of `RequestValidation.authenticate_client` done, use that validator for your token endpoint. Call the token endpoint with a body of 
```
{
  "client_id": <ID of the public client you made>,
  "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code",
  "device_code": <anything you want since it's not validated>
}
```

You now have a bearer token for the client without a valid `device_code`.

### Impact
Anyone using the RFC 8628 device workflow in oauthlib that doesn't realize the `device_code` parameter is not being validated.

### Summary

An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash a running MONAILabel server or silently corrupt its medical AI inference results by uploading a single crafted DICOM file (~132 KB) via the REST API. The vulnerability stems from pydicom's lack of validation for Decimal String (DS) and Integer String (IS) DICOM Value Representations, which allows NaN and infinity values to pass through MONAI's PydicomReader and propagate through the entire spatial transform and ML inference pipeline.

No authentication is required for the default MONAILabel REST API. The attacker needs only network access to the server (default port 8000).

**Severity:** CVSS 3.1: 8.7 HIGH  
**CVSS Vector:** CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:L  
**CWE:** CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) → CWE-682 (Incorrect Calculation)

### Details

**Root Cause — Layer 1: pydicom accepts invalid VR values**

pydicom's `DSfloat.__new__()` calls Python's `float(val)`, which silently accepts "NaN", "inf", and "-inf". The DICOM standard (PS3.5 Table 6.2-1) defines DS as digits 0-9, +, -, ., e only. NaN and inf are not valid DS values. The `is_valid_ds()` check only runs in RAISE validation mode, which is NOT the default. The default mode is WARN, which still returns the invalid value.

```python
>>> from pydicom.valuerep import DSfloat
>>> DSfloat("NaN")
nan    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
>>> DSfloat("inf")
inf    # Accepted silently — should be rejected
```

This affects ALL pydicom versions from 0.9.7 through 3.0.2 (current).

A related bypass exists in pydicom's IS type: `IS("1e4")` returns 10000 via an `int(float(val))` fallback, accepting scientific notation that is not valid per the DICOM standard.

**Root Cause — Layer 2: MONAI Core trusts pydicom output without validation**

MONAI's `PydicomReader._get_affine()` builds a 4x4 affine transformation matrix from PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, and ImageOrientationPatient with ZERO `isfinite()` or `isnan()` checks. NaN in PixelSpacing produces NaN in the affine diagonal, propagating through every spatial transform:
`PydicomReader._get_affine() → LoadImaged → Spacingd → Model → Writer`

**Root Cause — Layer 3: MONAILabel REST API accepts anything**

MONAILabel's `PUT /datastore/` endpoint accepts DICOM uploads with no authentication (default deployment), no validation of spatial metadata, and no bounds checking on any DICOM tag values. The malicious DICOM is stored permanently and made available for inference.

### PoC

**Environment Setup:**
```bash
# Start MONAILabel (Docker)
docker pull projectmonai/monailabel:latest
docker run -d --name monailabel-poc -p 8000:8000 --memory=8g \
    projectmonai/monailabel:latest monailabel start_server \
    --app /opt/monai/sample-apps/radiology \
    --studies /opt/monai/datasets/Task09_Spleen/imagesTr \
    --conf models segmentation

# Verify server is running
curl http://localhost:8000/info/
```

**Step 1 — Establish baseline (legitimate data works):**
```bash
curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/infer/segmentation?image=spleen_40" \
     -o baseline.nii.gz -w "HTTP %{http_code} - %{size_download} bytes"
# Result: HTTP 200, ~223,628 bytes valid segmentation mask
```

**Step 2 — Run the attack (NaN DICOM upload + inference):**
```bash
pip install pydicom numpy requests
python poc_monailabel_ds_bypass.py --server http://localhost:8000
```

The PoC script:
1. Confirms pydicom accepts NaN/inf in DS fields
2. 2. Creates three malicious DICOM files (~132 KB each) with NaN/inf in PixelSpacing and ImagePositionPatient
3. 3. Uploads each via `PUT /datastore/` (no auth required) — HTTP 200 accepted
4. 4. Triggers inference via `POST /infer/segmentation` — HTTP 500, server crash
**Demonstrated Results:**

| Payload | Upload | Inference | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (spleen_40) | N/A | HTTP 200 | Valid 223 KB segmentation |
| NaN PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (18.0s wasted compute) |
| NaN PixelSpacing + IPP | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.7s wasted compute) |
| Inf PixelSpacing | HTTP 200 | HTTP 500 | RuntimeError crash (16.4s wasted compute) |

**Server crash traceback:**
```
monailabel/tasks/infer/basic_infer.py → self.writer(data)
monailabel/transform/writer.py → write_itk(...)
itk/ITKCommonBasePython.py → itkProcessObject_Update()
RuntimeError: itkGDCMImageIO.cxx:1226:
  ITK ERROR: GDCMImageIO: A Floating point buffer was passed
  but the stored pixel type was not specified.
```

Each request burns ~16 seconds of server compute (full ML inference pipeline) before crashing. The NaN DICOM persists in the datastore — any future inference on that image ID crashes the server again.

**Library-level confirmation:** 17/17 test vectors confirmed against MONAI 1.5.2 and pydicom 3.0.2, including actual MONAI `LoadImaged` and `Spacingd` transforms accepting NaN geometry without error.

### Impact

1. **Denial of Service:** A single ~132 KB DICOM upload crashes the MONAILabel inference pipeline. All active inference requests from legitimate users are aborted. Repeatable indefinitely with minimal bandwidth.
2. **Silent Data Corruption:** NaN values in spatial metadata propagate through the entire ML inference pipeline and produce geometrically incorrect segmentation masks. If the output writer does not crash, the result is returned with HTTP 200 and zero warnings.
3. **Persistent Datastore Poisoning:** The malicious DICOM is stored permanently via `PUT /datastore/`. Any future inference request on that image ID reproduces the crash or corruption, persisting across server restarts.
**Affected MONAI Ecosystem (9 repositories):**
- MONAI Core: PydicomReader, LoadImaged, Spacingd transforms
- - MONAILabel: REST API + DICOMweb datastore
- - MONAI Deploy App SDK: DICOMDataLoaderOperator
- - model-zoo, VISTA, GenerativeModels, tutorials, research-contributions
**Affected DICOM Tags (any DS VR):** PixelSpacing, ImagePositionPatient, SliceThickness, ImageOrientationPatient, RescaleSlope, WindowCenter/WindowWidth

**Recommended Fix:**
1. Add `math.isfinite()` validation in `PydicomReader._get_affine()` on all values from PixelSpacing, IPP, IOP. Raise ValueError for NaN/inf.
2. 2. Validate spatial metadata of uploaded DICOM in MONAILabel `PUT /datastore/`. Return HTTP 400 for invalid geometry.
3. 3. Validate spatial metadata is finite in `LoadImaged`/`Spacingd` before resampling.
4. 4. Coordinate with pydicom upstream to reject NaN/inf in DS fields in all validation modes.
**Upstream:** pydicom GHSA filed 2026-04-05.

**Author:** Paulino Calderon (paulino@calderonpale.com)
The URL handler in the manual browser option for Gaim before 0.59.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary script via shell metacharacters in a link.

Implementations of SSH version 1.5, including (1) OpenSSH up to version 2.3.0, (2) AppGate, and (3) ssh-1 up to version 1.2.31, in certain configurations, allow a remote attacker to decrypt and/or alter traffic via a "Bleichenbacher attack" on PKCS#1 version 1.5.

Multiple stack-based buffer overflows in the ICQ parsing routines of the ISS Protocol Analysis Module (PAM) component, as used in various RealSecure, Proventia, and BlackICE products, allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a SRV_MULTI response containing a SRV_USER_ONLINE response packet and a SRV_META_USER response packet with long (1) nickname, (2) firstname, (3) lastname, or (4) email address fields, as exploited by the Witty worm.
Buffer overflow in GoAhead WebServer 2.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a long HTTP GET request with a large number of subdirectories.
PHP-Nuke 7.0 allows remote attackers to obtain the installation path via certain characters such as (1) ", (2) ', or (3) > in the search field, which reveals the path in an error message.

ZITADEL 4.x before 4.17.1 does not check an organization's inactive state during Login V2 authentication, verifying only the individual user's status. Users of a deactivated organization who hold valid credentials, an existing session, or a refresh token can still sign in, create sessions, and obtain or refresh tokens.
Unknown vulnerability in the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) in Windows 2000 domain controllers allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted LDAP message.

Buffer overflow in the Private Communications Transport (PCT) protocol implementation in the Microsoft SSL library, as used in Microsoft Windows NT 4.0 SP6a, 2000 SP2 through SP4, XP SP1, Server 2003, NetMeeting, Windows 98, and Windows ME, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via PCT 1.0 handshake packets.

In Video HAL, there is a possible escalation of privilege due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Patch ID: ALPS11375674; Issue ID: MSV-9571.

In Modem, there is a possible out of bounds read due to a missing bounds check. This could lead to remote denial of service, if a UE has connected to a rogue base station controlled by the attacker, with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Patch ID: MOLY01774038; Issue ID: MSV-8912.

In aidl, there is a possible memory corruption due to use after free. This could lead to local escalation of privilege if a malicious actor has already obtained the System privilege. User interaction is not needed for exploitation. Patch ID: ALPS11242428; Issue ID: MSV-9038.
The default configuration for UUCP in AIX before 3.2 allows local users to gain root privileges.
Auto_FTP.pl script in Auto_FTP 0.2 stores usernames and passwords in plaintext in the auto_ftp.conf configuration file.

Auto_FTP.pl script in Auto_FTP 0.2 uses the /tmp/ftp_tmp as a shared directory with insecure permissions, which allows local users to (1) send arbitrary files to the remote server by placing them in the directory, and (2) view files that are being transferred.
umb-scheme 3.2-11 for Red Hat Linux is installed with world-writeable files.
DiskCheck script diskcheck.pl in Red Hat Linux 6.2 allows local users to create or overwrite arbitrary files via a symlink attack on a temporary file.
